decks.title: Business Environment — Part 1: Meaning, Features and Importance
goals: Explain the meaning of business environment and tell specific forces from general forces
Explain the features of business environment and identify them in a case
Explain why understanding the environment matters for a business

slides.heading: Business Environment
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what the business environment is, its **features**, and why firms must **understand** it.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: meaning, specific and general forces, features, importance
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to Business Environment. No business works in a vacuum. Customers change their tastes, rivals launch new products, banks change interest rates and governments make new rules. In this part we see what the business environment means, what its features are, and why every manager, from a small shop owner to a large company head, must keep watching it.

slides.heading: What is business environment?
slides.body_md: The **business environment** is the sum of all **individuals, institutions and other forces outside** a business that are beyond its control but may affect its performance.

rows: Its own products, prices and policies
Economic, social, technological, political and legal conditions
Outside the control of any single firm

visual.alt: Table contrasting what lies inside a firm (owners, staff, machines, its own policies, under its control) with the business environment outside it (customers, suppliers, competitors, investors and the general conditions, outside its control)

slides.narration: Draw a line around a firm. Everything inside, such as the owners, staff, machines and the firm's own policies, is largely under management's control. Everything outside the line that can affect the firm is its business environment: customers, suppliers, rivals, investors, and the wider economic, social, technological, political and legal conditions. The key words are external and beyond control.

visual.alt: Diagram of the business environment as rings around a firm: the inner ring holds specific forces (customers, suppliers, competitors, investors) that act directly; the outer ring holds general forces (economic, social, technological, political, legal) that act indirectly
visual.caption: Specific forces touch one firm directly; general forces touch every firm indirectly.

slides.narration: Picture the firm at the centre of two rings. The inner ring holds specific forces such as customers, suppliers, competitors and investors. They deal with the firm directly, almost every day. The outer ring holds general forces: economic, social, technological, political and legal conditions. They affect all firms, but indirectly. A supplier's strike hits one firm; a rise in interest rates touches everyone.

slides.heading: Quick check: general or specific?
slides.body_md: Which one of these is a **general** force?
slides.narration: Ask whether the force deals with one firm directly, or whether it affects all firms in an indirect way.

slides.heading: Features (1): totality, specific and general, inter-relatedness

rows: The sum of all forces outside the firm, taken together
Buyers, rivals, laws and technology all at once
Some act on one firm directly; others on all firms indirectly
A supplier's delay vs a change in interest rates
A change in one force sets off changes in others
A tax change alters prices, demand and advertising

visual.alt: Table of three features of business environment: totality of external forces, specific and general forces, and inter-relatedness, with meanings and illustrations

slides.narration: The environment has several features. First, totality: it is the sum of all external forces taken together. Second, it has both specific and general forces. Third, the forces are inter-related. A change in one sets off changes in others. For instance, a new tax may change prices, which changes demand, which changes how firms advertise.

slides.heading: Features (2): dynamic, uncertain, complex, relative

rows: Phone models outdated within a year or two
Future changes are hard to predict
Will this season's colours sell next year?
Many forces, hard to understand together
How an election, a drought and a new app combine
Its effect differs by place and firm
Raincoats sell in Kerala in June, not in Rajasthan

visual.alt: Table of four more features of business environment: dynamic nature, uncertainty, complexity and relativity, with meanings and illustrations

slides.narration: Four more features. The environment is dynamic: it keeps changing. It is uncertain: the future is hard to predict, especially in fashion and technology. It is complex: there are so many forces that their combined effect is hard to understand. And it is relative: the same force can have a different effect in different places, or on different firms.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the feature
slides.body_md: Woollen jackets sell more in Ladakh but not in Chennai. Which feature is this?
slides.narration: The same change, a different result in two places. Which feature describes that?

slides.heading: Inter-relatedness in action

visual.alt: Flow showing inter-relatedness: growing health awareness, a social change, raises demand for baked snacks, which leads firms to adopt new ovens, and labelling rules then tighten
visual.caption: One change ripples through the others

slides.narration: Here is inter-relatedness in action. As people become more health conscious, a social change, demand for baked snacks rises, an economic change. Firms buy new ovens, a technological change, and the government tightens labelling rules, a legal change. So a manager can never look at one force in isolation; one change ripples through the others.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: spotting features in a case
slides.body_md: Board questions often quote lines from a case and ask you to name the feature.
bullets: Step 1 — Read each line and ask what it says about the environment: change, unpredictability, place-to-place difference, linked forces?
Step 2 — Name the **feature** exactly.
Step 3 — Quote the line and give the **reason** in a few words.

headers: Line in the case (imagined toy maker, Channapatna)
rows: "Our buyers abroad and our buyers in Mysuru react quite differently to the same price rise"
Same force, different effect by place
"Nobody can say whether wooden toys will stay in fashion"
The future is hard to predict
"Each year brings a new design trend"

visual.alt: Worked example table: three lines from an imagined toy maker in Channapatna matched to the features relativity, uncertainty and dynamic nature, with reasons
visual.caption: Quote the line, name the feature, give the reason.

slides.narration: Let us practise with an imagined toy maker in Channapatna. When the owner says buyers abroad and buyers in Mysuru react differently to the same price rise, that is relativity. When she says nobody can tell whether wooden toys will stay in fashion, that is uncertainty. When each year brings a new design trend, that is the dynamic nature. Always quote the line, name the feature and give a reason.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Business environment is complex because its many forces and their combined effect are hard to understand.
slides.narration: Think about what makes the environment difficult to understand completely.

slides.heading: Why understand the environment? (1)
columns:
**Opportunities**

- Spot new needs early
- Act before rivals
- Gain the **first-mover advantage**

**Threats**

- Notice coming dangers
- New rivals, rules, shortages
- Use **early warning signals** to prepare

visual.alt: Flow: scanning the environment leads either to an opportunity, where the firm acts first and gains the first-mover advantage, or to a threat, where it prepares early using early warning signals
visual.caption: Two sides of the same habit

slides.narration: Why should managers study the environment? First, to identify opportunities. A firm that spots a new need early and acts first gains the first-mover advantage. Second, to identify threats. News of a powerful new rival, a stricter rule or a shortage of raw material is an early warning signal; the firm that notices it can prepare before the damage is done.

slides.heading: Why understand the environment? (2)

rows: Finance, material, machines, people on better terms
Adapting in time rather than being surprised
A sound basis for goals and courses of action

visual.alt: Table of six benefits of understanding the business environment: identifying opportunities, identifying threats, tapping resources, coping with rapid changes, planning and policy formulation, and improving performance

slides.narration: There are more reasons. The environment is the source of a firm's resources such as finance, raw material, machines and people, so understanding it helps tap them on better terms. It helps a firm cope with rapid changes in a fast-moving market. It gives a sound basis for planning and policy formulation. And all of this together improves performance over time.

slides.heading: Quick check: which benefit?
slides.body_md: A firm launches a millet mix before any rival and becomes the best-known brand. Which benefit did it gain?
slides.narration: The firm saw a need early and acted before others. Which benefit is that?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: applying the benefits
slides.body_md: Match each situation at an imagined dairy in Anand with the benefit it shows.
bullets: Step 1 — Is the dairy **gaining** something new (opportunity) or **avoiding** harm (threat)?
Step 2 — Is it about **inputs** (resources), **speed of change** (coping), or **future plans** (planning)?
Step 3 — Write the benefit and point to the words in the situation.

headers: Situation at an imagined dairy in Anand
rows: Spots demand for lactose-free milk before rivals
Learns early that a big rival will open a plant nearby
Gets a cheaper loan by tracking bank schemes
Shifts to online orders as habits change

visual.alt: Worked example table applying four benefits of understanding the environment to an imagined dairy in Anand
visual.caption: Name the benefit and point to the line that shows it.

slides.narration: Here is how to apply the benefits. Spotting demand for lactose-free milk before rivals is an opportunity with the first-mover advantage. Hearing early that a large rival will open a plant nearby is a threat noticed in time. Getting a cheaper loan by tracking bank schemes is tapping resources. Moving to online orders as habits change is coping with rapid change.

slides.heading: How firms respond to change

visual.alt: Flow of how a firm responds to its environment: notice the change, judge whether it is an opportunity or a threat, revise plans, then act and review
visual.caption: Responding to change

slides.narration: Good firms follow a simple cycle. They notice the change by scanning the environment. They judge whether it is an opportunity or a threat for them. They revise their plans and policies. Then they act, and keep watching the results, because the environment will change again. This is why environmental study is a continuous habit, not a one-time exercise.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: All external forces that can affect a business
Totality, specific and general, inter-related, dynamic, uncertain, complex, relative
Opportunities, threats, resources, coping with change, planning, performance

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning, seven features and six benefits of understanding the business environment

slides.narration: To sum up. The business environment is the total of all external forces that may affect a business. It has specific forces acting directly and general forces acting indirectly. Its features are totality, specific and general forces, inter-relatedness, dynamic nature, uncertainty, complexity and relativity. Understanding it helps a firm find opportunities, avoid threats, tap resources, cope with change, plan, and perform better.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Use the word **external**: the environment is outside the firm and beyond its control.
In case questions, **quote the exact line** before naming the feature or benefit.
Do not confuse **relativity** (differs by place or firm) with **uncertainty** (future unknown).
Opportunities go with the **first-mover advantage**; threats go with **early warning signals**.
5-mark questions: five named points, each with one line of explanation.
slides.narration: A few tips. Always describe the environment as external and beyond the firm's control. In case questions, quote the exact line first, then name the feature or benefit. Keep relativity and uncertainty apart. Pair opportunities with the first-mover advantage, and threats with early warning signals. For five marks, write five named points with a line of explanation each.

decks.title: Business Environment — Part 2: Dimensions and Demonetisation
goals: Classify changes into the economic, social, technological, political and legal dimensions
Distinguish the political environment from the legal environment
Explain the concept and features of demonetisation and how it affected businesses

slides.heading: Dimensions of business environment
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the **five dimensions** of the general environment, and **demonetisation** (2016).

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the five dimensions of business environment, then demonetisation
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 2 we look closely at the general environment, which has five dimensions: economic, social, technological, political and legal. Then we study one real change that affected almost every Indian business at the same time: the withdrawal of the old five hundred and one thousand rupee notes in November 2016.

slides.heading: The five dimensions

rows: Interest rates, inflation, incomes, money supply, stock market, tax rates
Customs, traditions, values, lifestyles, health and education levels
Scientific improvements and innovations: new ways of producing and delivering
Stability of government, law and order, government's attitude to business
Acts, rules and court decisions that business must follow

visual.alt: Table of the five dimensions of business environment and what each includes: economic, social, technological, political and legal

slides.narration: Here are the five dimensions. Economic covers interest rates, inflation, incomes and tax rates. Social covers customs, values and lifestyles. Technological covers new inventions and methods. Political covers the stability of government and its attitude towards business. Legal covers the acts, rules and court decisions that firms must obey. Learn one clear example for each.

slides.heading: Economic environment

rows: Cheaper loans: more investment and credit buying
Costs rise; buyers may cut spending
Demand rises for many goods and services

visual.alt: Table of economic changes and their likely effects: falling interest rates encourage investment and credit buying, rising inflation raises costs, rising incomes raise demand

slides.narration: The economic environment matters most directly for costs and demand. When interest rates fall, loans become cheaper, so firms invest more and customers buy homes and cars on credit. When inflation rises, raw material and wages cost more, and buyers may cut back. When incomes rise, demand rises for many goods and services.

slides.heading: Social environment

rows: Creches, ready-to-cook food, home services grow
Seasonal demand for sweets, lamps, clothes

visual.alt: Table of social changes and business responses: more women in paid work, greater health awareness, and festivals and traditions

slides.narration: The social environment is about people: their customs, traditions, values and ways of living. As more women take up paid work, demand grows for creches and ready-to-cook food. Health awareness lifts gyms and low-sugar foods. Festivals create seasonal demand for sweets, lamps and clothes. A firm that reads these changes well can design the right products.

slides.heading: Technological environment

nodes.label: Firms that adopt it gain new customers (opportunity)
Firms with outdated products lose sales (threat)

visual.alt: Flow: new technology creates an opportunity for firms that adopt it and a threat for firms whose products become outdated
visual.caption: Technology cuts both ways

slides.narration: The technological environment covers scientific improvements and innovations that give new ways of making and delivering goods and services. Technology cuts both ways. Firms that adopt a new method or product early gain customers, while firms that stay with outdated products lose sales. Think of how phone cameras affected the makers of film rolls.

slides.heading: Quick check: which dimension?
slides.body_md: Shopkeepers start accepting payments by QR code. Which dimension is this?
slides.narration: A new way of doing a familiar task. Which dimension does that belong to?

slides.heading: Political and legal environment
columns:
**Political**

- Stability of government
- Law and order
- Government's attitude to business

**Legal**

- Acts passed by the legislature
- Rules made by the government
- Court decisions

rows: Political conditions: stability, law and order, attitude to business
Shaping confidence and the business climate
A stable state government invites investors
A rule makes safety labels compulsory

visual.alt: Table contrasting the political environment (stability, law and order, government attitude; shapes confidence) with the legal environment (acts, rules, court decisions; binds firms), with examples

slides.narration: Students often mix up these two. The political environment is about political conditions: whether the government is stable, whether there is peace and law and order, and whether the government welcomes business. The legal environment is about the actual laws, rules and court decisions that firms are bound to follow. In short, one sets the mood for investment, while the other lays down what firms must do.

slides.heading: Quick check: fill in the blank
slides.body_md: Inflation, interest rates and money supply belong to which environment?
slides.narration: These are all about money, prices and credit. Name the dimension.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: classifying changes
slides.body_md: An imagined tea company in Darjeeling faces four changes. Classify each.
bullets: Step 1 — Money, prices, wages or credit? **Economic**.
Step 2 — People's tastes, values, habits? **Social**.
Step 3 — New methods or machines? **Technological**.
Step 4 — Government conditions? **Political**. A binding rule or court order? **Legal**.

headers: Change faced by an imagined tea company in Darjeeling
rows: Wages of plantation workers rise across the region
City buyers prefer green tea for health
Drones are used to spray and monitor bushes
A new rule requires the origin to be printed on every pack

visual.alt: Worked example table classifying four changes faced by an imagined tea company: rising wages (economic), preference for green tea (social), drones (technological), origin labelling rule (legal)
visual.caption: Ask: is it about money, people, methods, government conditions, or a binding rule?

slides.narration: Let us classify four changes for an imagined tea company. Rising wages across the region is about costs, so economic. City buyers preferring green tea for health is about tastes, so social. Drones that spray and monitor the bushes are a new method, so technological. A rule that the origin must be printed on every pack is a binding rule, so legal.

slides.heading: One change, many dimensions

visual.alt: Flow of one change rippling across dimensions: cheap phones and data lead to online shopping habits, online sellers gain sales, and rules on online consumer rights follow
visual.caption: The dimensions are inter-related

slides.narration: Remember that the dimensions are inter-related. Cheap phones and data, a technological change, changed shopping habits, a social change. Online sellers gained sales, an economic change, and new rules followed to protect online buyers, a legal change. In a long answer, showing this chain earns marks for understanding, not just for listing.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the changes
slides.body_md: Match each change faced by an imagined lamp maker with its dimension.
slides.narration: Take each change in turn and ask the same five questions you used in the worked example.

slides.heading: Demonetisation: what happened

rows: 8 November 2016, by the Government of India
Deposited them in banks or exchanged them within a time limit; new notes were issued

visual.alt: Table of demonetisation facts: announced 8 November 2016; old 500 and 1,000 rupee notes stopped being legal tender; people deposited or exchanged them within a time limit

slides.narration: Now a change that touched almost every business together. On the eighth of November 2016, the Government of India announced that the then existing five hundred and one thousand rupee notes would stop being legal tender. People had to deposit them in banks or exchange them within a time limit, and new notes were issued over the following weeks.

slides.heading: Features of demonetisation

rows: Cash comes into banks, so incomes can be checked
Curb black money and fake notes
Unaccounted and counterfeit cash is exposed
Money kept at home moves into banks and can be lent

visual.alt: Table of features of demonetisation: tax administration measure, curbing black money and fake notes, push to a less-cash economy, formalisation of savings

slides.narration: Its stated features and aims were these. It was a tax administration measure, because cash had to come into banks where incomes could be checked. It aimed to curb black money and counterfeit notes. It pushed the economy towards fewer cash payments and more digital ones. And it moved savings kept at home into the formal banking system.

slides.heading: Quick check: what did it mean?
slides.body_md: What did demonetisation of the old notes mean for a business in practice?
slides.narration: Think about whether the old notes could still be used to pay, and what holders had to do.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading payment data
slides.body_md: An imagined chemist's monthly receipts (₹ thousand): before, cash 170 and digital 30; after, cash 120 and digital 80.
bullets: Step 2 — Digital share before: 30 ÷ 200 × 100 = 15 per cent.
Step 3 — Digital share after: 80 ÷ 200 × 100 = 40 per cent.
Step 4 — Link to a feature: the **push to a less-cash, digital economy**.

slides.heading: Effects on business
columns:
**Short term**

- Cash shortage
- Lower sales for cash-based trade
- Time lost in bank queues

**Longer term**

- More digital payments
- More formal accounts and records
- More savings in banks

rows: More firms with bank accounts and formal records

visual.alt: Table of effects of demonetisation on business: short-term cash shortage, lower sales and lost time; longer-term wider digital payments, more formal records and more bank savings

slides.narration: For businesses the effects came in two stages. In the short term, cash was scarce, so trades that depended on cash saw lower sales, and owners lost time in bank queues. Over a longer period, more businesses accepted digital payments, kept formal records and held their money in banks. In the exam, describe these effects in neutral terms.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Conditions and attitude vs binding rules
8 Nov 2016; old ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes; tax administration, less cash, formalisation

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: five dimensions, the political versus legal distinction, and the key points of demonetisation

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. The general environment has five dimensions: economic, social, technological, political and legal. Political means conditions and attitude; legal means binding rules and court decisions. Demonetisation, announced on the eighth of November 2016, withdrew the old five hundred and one thousand rupee notes as legal tender; its features were tax administration, curbing black money and fake notes, less cash, and formalisation of savings.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Classify by asking: money, people, methods, government conditions, or a binding rule?
A **rule or court order** is **legal**, even if the government made it; stability and attitude are **political**.
Demonetisation: **8 November 2016**, old **₹500 and ₹1,000** notes; do not mix it up with **GST** (2017).
For demonetisation, write **features** in neutral language; do not give a personal verdict.
In case questions, quote the line, then name the dimension or feature.
slides.narration: Final tips. To classify a change, ask whether it is about money, people, methods, government conditions, or a binding rule. A rule or a court order is legal, even when the government made it. Remember the date and notes for demonetisation, and do not confuse it with the Goods and Services Tax of 2017. Write its features in neutral language, and always quote the line in case questions.

notes.title: Business Environment — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Meaning: specific and general forces
sections.body_md:
The **business environment** is the sum of all individuals, institutions and other forces **outside** a business that it **cannot control** but that may affect its working.

- **Specific forces** act on an individual firm **directly** in its daily working: customers, suppliers, competitors, investors.
- **General forces** act on **all** firms, **indirectly**: economic, social, technological, political and legal conditions.

The firm itself (owners, staff, machines, its own policies) is **not** part of the environment.

key_terms.definition_md: All external individuals, institutions and forces that may affect a business and lie beyond its control.
Customers, suppliers, competitors and investors, who affect a firm directly.
Economic, social, technological, political and legal conditions that affect all firms indirectly.

sections.heading: 2. Features of business environment
sections.body_md:
1. **Totality of external forces**: the aggregate of everything outside the firm.
2. **Specific and general forces**: direct and indirect influences.
3. **Inter-relatedness**: forces affect one another; one change sets off others.
4. **Dynamic nature**: it keeps changing (technology, tastes, competition, policy).
5. **Uncertainty**: future conditions are hard to predict, especially in fashion and IT.
6. **Complexity**: many forces whose combined effect is hard to grasp.
7. **Relativity**: the effect of a force differs from place to place and firm to firm.

key_terms.definition_md: The feature that a change in one environmental force leads to changes in others.

sections.heading: 3. Importance of understanding the environment
sections.body_md:
1. **Identifying opportunities and the first-mover advantage**: acting early on new needs.
2. **Identifying threats and early warning signals**: preparing for new rivals, rules or shortages.
3. **Tapping useful resources**: inputs such as finance, raw material, machines and labour come from the environment.
4. **Coping with rapid changes**: adapting in time in a fast-changing market.
5. **Assistance in planning and policy formulation**: opportunities and threats are the basis of plans.
6. **Improving performance**: firms that monitor the environment do better over time.

Because the environment is dynamic, studying it must be a **continuous** process.

sections.heading: 4. Economic, social and technological dimensions
sections.body_md:
- **Economic environment**: interest rates, inflation, disposable income, money supply, the stock market, tax rates. These shape **costs and demand**.
- **Social environment**: customs, traditions, values, lifestyles, health and education levels, population trends. These shape **what people buy**.
- **Technological environment**: scientific improvements and innovations that give new ways of producing and delivering goods and services. They create **opportunities** for firms that adopt them and **threats** for firms with outdated products.

sections.heading: 5. Political and legal dimensions
sections.body_md:
- **Political environment**: political conditions such as general stability and peace, law and order, and the attitude of the government towards business. These shape **business confidence**.
- **Legal environment**: legislation passed by Parliament and state legislatures, rules and orders of the government, and **decisions of courts**. Firms are **bound** to comply.

The five dimensions are **inter-related**: a technological change can alter habits (social), sales (economic) and later rules (legal).

sections.heading: 6. Demonetisation (2016)
sections.body_md:
**Concept:** on **8 November 2016** the Government of India withdrew the **legal-tender** status of the then existing **₹500 and ₹1,000** notes. Holders had to deposit or exchange them within a time limit; new notes were issued.

**Features and stated aims:**
1. A **tax administration measure**: cash moved into banks, where incomes could be traced.
2. To curb **black money** and **counterfeit** currency.
3. A push towards a **less-cash, digital** economy (cards, wallets, transfers).
4. **Formalisation of savings**: money held at home moved into the banking system.

**Effects on business:** a short-term **shortage of cash** hit cash-based trade; over time more firms accepted **digital payments** and kept **formal records**. Describe these effects in neutral terms.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Including the firm's own staff or machines in its environment: the environment is **external**.
- Calling a binding rule "political": acts, rules and court orders are **legal**; stability and attitude are **political**.
- Mixing up **relativity** (effect differs by place or firm) and **uncertainty** (future cannot be predicted).
- Confusing demonetisation (**8 November 2016**, notes) with **GST** (1 July 2017, taxes).
- Writing a personal verdict on demonetisation instead of its **features** and effects.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: correct option, or the correct feature or dimension.
- 3–4 mark case parts: **quote the line**, name the feature/dimension/benefit, explain briefly.
- 5 marks: five named points, each explained in a line, about 80–120 words.

questions.stem_md: In Business Studies, the term **business environment** refers to

options.text_md: the office building, machines and furniture of a business
the total of all individuals, institutions and other forces outside a business that may affect its performance
the relations among the employees working inside one firm
only the customers who buy the products of a business

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the total of all individuals, institutions and other forces outside a business that may affect its performance. Business environment means the sum of all **external** forces (individuals, institutions and other forces) that lie outside the control of a business but may affect it. Buildings and staff relations are internal; customers are only one part of it.

questions.stem_md: Rangoli Paints (an imagined firm in Pune) notices that its two main suppliers of titanium dioxide have raised prices, and a rival has opened a depot next door. These forces are examples of

options.text_md: general forces
internal forces
controllable forces
specific forces

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** specific forces. Suppliers and competitors affect an individual firm **directly** in its day-to-day working, so they are **specific** forces. General forces (economic, social, political, legal, technological) affect all firms indirectly. Neither group is internal or under the firm's control.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a **general** force of the business environment?

options.text_md: A change in the social attitudes of people towards healthy food
A firm's regular customers asking for faster delivery
A supplier delaying the delivery of raw material to one factory
A local investor offering to buy shares of a particular company

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A change in the social attitudes of people towards healthy food. A change in social attitudes affects **all** firms, though indirectly, so it is a general force. Customers, suppliers and investors deal with one firm directly; they are specific forces.

questions.stem_md: A rise in demand for woollen jackets in Ladakh does not change demand for them in coastal Chennai. Which feature of business environment does this illustrate?

options.text_md: Inter-relatedness
Totality of external forces
Relativity
Complexity

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Relativity. The impact of environmental forces **differs from place to place** (and from firm to firm). This is **relativity**. Inter-relatedness is about forces affecting each other; totality is about the sum of forces; complexity is about how hard the forces are to understand.

questions.stem_md: Business environment is called **dynamic** because

options.text_md: it can be fully controlled by the top management of a firm
it affects only large companies and never small firms
it keeps changing all the time, in technology, tastes, competition and government policy
its future course can be predicted exactly

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** it keeps changing all the time, in technology, tastes, competition and government policy. Dynamic means **constantly changing**. The environment is outside a firm's control, affects firms of every size, and its future is uncertain, so the other options describe the opposite.

questions.stem_md: A fashion brand in Surat (imagined) cannot tell whether this winter's colours will still be popular next year. This shows which feature of business environment?

options.text_md: Uncertainty
Relativity
Specific and general forces
Totality of external forces

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Uncertainty. Future conditions are **hard to predict**, especially in fast-changing fields such as fashion and technology. That is **uncertainty**.

questions.stem_md: Dhruv Agro (imagined) spotted early that city families wanted ready-to-cook millet mixes, launched one before any rival and became the best-known brand. Which benefit of understanding the environment did it gain?

options.text_md: Identifying threats and getting early warning signals
Tapping useful resources
Assistance in planning only for the next week
Identifying opportunities and getting the first-mover advantage

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Identifying opportunities and getting the first-mover advantage. Spotting a new demand before others and acting on it first gives the **first-mover advantage**, the benefit of identifying opportunities. Early warning signals are about threats; tapping resources is about inputs such as finance and raw material.

questions.stem_md: Seeing that two foreign brands were about to enter India with cheaper electric scooters, Vidyut Motors (imagined) cut costs, improved after-sales service and advertised its local network. This illustrates the importance of business environment in

options.text_md: identifying opportunities and getting the first-mover advantage
identifying threats and early warning signals
tapping useful resources
improving the image of the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** identifying threats and early warning signals. The coming competition is a **threat**; reading it early lets the firm prepare. That is the benefit of **identifying threats and early warning signals**.

questions.stem_md: Business environment is a **source of inputs** such as finance, machines, raw material and labour, and a business supplies outputs to it. This explains why understanding it helps in

options.text_md: tapping useful resources
improving performance only through advertising
reducing competition by law
avoiding all risks

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** tapping useful resources. A firm gets its **resources** from the environment and must understand it to obtain them on good terms. No firm can avoid all risks or reduce competition simply by understanding the environment.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is **NOT** a feature of business environment?

options.text_md: It is dynamic
It is fully under the control of the business
It is complex
It is relative

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It is fully under the control of the business. The environment consists of **external** forces that a firm **cannot control**; it can only adapt to them. Dynamic, complex and relative are all features.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Different forces of business environment are closely inter-related.

**Reason (R):** A rise in health awareness, a social change, can increase demand for fitness trackers and push firms to adopt new sensor technology.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: one social change sets off economic (demand) and technological (new products) changes, showing that the forces are **inter-related**.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A firm can change its business environment whenever it wishes.

**Reason (R):** Business environment consists of forces that are outside the control of an individual business.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: the environment is external and a single firm cannot change it at will; it can only respond. R is true.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Firms that keep studying their environment usually perform better over time.

**Reason (R):** Business environment includes both specific forces and general forces.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. A is true because such firms adjust their plans in time; R merely classifies the forces.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Business environment is complex because it is made up of many inter-related and changing forces whose combined effect is hard to understand fully.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** This is the meaning of **complexity**: it is easy to list the forces but hard to understand how together they will affect a business.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Only large companies need to understand their business environment; small firms are not affected by it.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Every business, large or small, operates in the environment and is affected by it; small firms may even be **more** vulnerable because they have fewer resources to absorb shocks.

questions.stem_md: Business environment is the sum or aggregate of all things external to a firm. This feature is called the ___ of external forces.
questions.solution_md: This feature is called the **totality** of external forces.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined situation with the feature of business environment it shows best.

options.text_md: A new tax rule makes a firm also revise its prices and its advertising
Mobile phone models become outdated within a year or two
Demand for raincoats rises in Kerala in June but not in Rajasthan
A firm cannot predict how a coming election will change its sales

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). One change sets off others (inter-relatedness); constant change (dynamic); different effect in different places (relativity); future hard to predict (uncertainty).

questions.stem_md: How do specific forces of business environment differ from general forces? Give one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Contrast direct vs indirect effect and individual firm vs all firms, with one example each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Specific forces** affect an individual firm **directly** in its day-to-day working, e.g. its **customers, suppliers, competitors and investors**. **General forces** affect **all** firms, **indirectly**, e.g. **economic, social, political, legal and technological** conditions.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three features of business environment.
questions.solution_md: Any three of: totality, specific and general forces, inter-relatedness, dynamic, uncertainty, complexity, relativity, each with a short explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Totality of external forces:** it is the sum of all forces outside the firm, taken together.
2. **Dynamic nature:** it keeps changing in technology, tastes, competition and policy.
3. **Uncertainty:** future changes are hard to predict, especially in fast-moving fields such as IT and fashion.

questions.stem_md: Pankhuri Cosmetics (imagined) studies market reports, government notices and social-media trends every month. Explain three ways in which this habit helps the firm.

questions.stem_md: "Understanding the business environment is essential for the success of a business." Explain any five reasons in support of this statement.
questions.solution_md: Five distinct points with a line of explanation each.

answer.model_answer_md:

2. **Identifying threats and early warning signals:** firms can prepare for new rivals, rules or shortages.
3. **Tapping useful resources:** finance, raw material, machines and labour come from the environment.
4. **Coping with rapid changes:** firms that watch the environment adapt in time instead of being surprised.
5. **Assistance in planning and policy formulation:** knowledge of opportunities and threats is the basis of future plans. (Also: **improving performance** over time.)

questions.stem_md: Explain any five features of business environment, with a short illustration of each.

2. **Social:** values and lifestyles; e.g. more people cycling for fitness raises demand.
3. **Technological:** new methods; e.g. electric-assist motors create a new product line.

questions.stem_md: For a business, what did demonetisation of the old ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes mean in practice?

Those notes became more valuable and were kept as savings

Prices of all goods were fixed by the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Those notes could no longer be used as legal tender for payments and had to be deposited or exchanged within a time limit. Demonetisation withdrew the **legal-tender** status of the notes: they stopped being valid money for payments and holders had to deposit or exchange them within a set period.

questions.stem_md: Demonetisation is described as a **tax administration measure** mainly because

options.text_md: it reduced every tax rate in the country
it abolished income tax for small traders
cash holdings had to be brought into banks, where they became traceable and could be checked against declared income
it replaced all indirect taxes with one tax

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** cash holdings had to be brought into banks, where they became traceable and could be checked against declared income. Old notes had to be deposited in bank accounts, so **unaccounted cash** came into the formal system where it could be checked against declared incomes. It did not change tax rates; replacing indirect taxes describes GST.

questions.stem_md: After November 2016, a chemist in Nagpur (imagined) started accepting payment through mobile wallets and card machines. Which stated feature of demonetisation does this reflect?

A push towards a less-cash, digital economy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A push towards a less-cash, digital economy. One stated aim was to **encourage digital transactions** and reduce dependence on cash; the chemist's switch reflects that.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an example of the **formalisation of savings** linked to demonetisation?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A household deposits cash it kept at home into a bank account, from which it later earns interest. Moving idle cash from homes into **banks** brings savings into the formal financial system, where they can be lent out for investment. The other options keep money outside the formal system.

Fake notes of the old series would be detected and become useless when people deposited or exchanged them

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Fake notes of the old series would be detected and become useless when people deposited or exchanged them. When every old note had to pass through a bank, **counterfeit** notes of that series could be identified and taken out of circulation.

questions.stem_md: Explain one short-term difficulty and one longer-term change that demonetisation brought for small retailers.

answer.model_answer_md: **Short term:** a sudden **shortage of cash** reduced sales for shops whose customers paid in cash. **Longer term:** many shops began accepting **digital payments**, which made their sales records more formal and traceable.

questions.stem_md: Explain three stated objectives behind withdrawing the old high-value notes in November 2016.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct objectives with a line of explanation each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Curb black money:** unaccounted cash had to come into banks, where it could be checked.
2. **Remove counterfeit notes:** fake notes of the old series were caught when deposited or exchanged.
3. **Encourage digital transactions:** a less-cash economy makes payments traceable and reduces cash handling.

questions.stem_md: Explain the concept of demonetisation and analyse how it changed the business environment for Indian firms, giving both its intended features and the adjustments firms had to make.
questions.solution_md: Concept, three features, and the adjustment firms faced, in neutral terms.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Concept:** on **8 November 2016** the government withdrew the legal-tender status of the old **₹500 and ₹1,000** notes; they had to be deposited or exchanged.
2. **Tax administration:** cash came into banks, making incomes **traceable**.
3. **Less-cash economy:** firms and customers moved towards **digital payments**.
4. **Formalisation:** savings and transactions shifted into the **formal** banking system.
5. **Adjustments:** cash-based firms faced a **temporary shortage** of cash and lower sales, and had to open accounts, accept digital payments and keep better records.
